problem: 'universally remarked' rendered 'People everywhere', which shifts from 'generally/by everyone' to a spatial claim
replacement: It has been widely remarked that in our time the members of a family stand on an entirely new footing with one another. The distance that once separated a father from his sons has shrunk, and paternal authority, if not destroyed, is at least weakened. Something similar, but even more striking, can be seen in the United States. In America the family, in the Roman and aristocratic sense of the word, does not exist. Only a few traces of it remain in the first years of childhood, when the father exercises, without opposition, the absolute domestic authority that his children’s helplessness makes necessary, and that both their interest and his own undeniable superiority justify. But as soon as the young American nears manhood, the bonds of filial obedience loosen day by day. Master of his thoughts, he soon becomes master of his conduct. Strictly speaking, America has no adolescence: when boyhood ends, the man appears and begins to mark out his own path. It would be a mistake to imagine that a domestic struggle comes first, in which the son wins by a kind of moral violence the liberty his father denied him. The same habits and the same principles that drive the one to assert his independence dispose the other to regard the use of that independence as an undeniable right. The son shows none of the rancorous or unruly passions that trouble men long after they have thrown off an established authority; the father feels none of the bitter, angry regret that tends to outlast a vanished power. The father foresees the limits of his authority long in advance, and when the time comes he gives it up without a fight. The son looks ahead to the exact moment when he will be his own master, and he enters into his freedom without haste and without effort, as a possession that is his own and that no one tries to wrest from him. *a

problem: 'easy shelter' rendered 'safe shelter' (changes the sense of comfortable/easy to secure)
replacement: [Footnote a: The Americans, however, have not yet seen fit to strip the parent of one of the chief elements of parental authority, as has been done in France, by depriving him of the power to dispose of his property at his death. In the United States a testator’s powers have no restrictions. In this respect, as in almost all others, it is easy to see that although the political legislation of the Americans is much more democratic than that of the French, the civil legislation of the French is infinitely more democratic than that of the Americans. There is an easy explanation. The civil legislation of France was the work of a man who saw that it served his interest to satisfy the democratic passions of his contemporaries in everything that was not directly and immediately hostile to his own power. He was willing to let some popular principles govern the distribution of property and the government of families, so long as they were not brought into the administration of public affairs. While the torrent of democracy swept over the civil laws of the country, he hoped to find an easy shelter behind its political institutions. This policy was both adroit and selfish. But a compromise of this kind could not last, because in the end political institutions always become the image and expression of civil society. In this sense it can be said that nothing in a nation is more political than its civil legislation.]

Perhaps nothing contributes more to changing the relations between a father and his children than the division of estates that democracy brings with it. When the father of a family has little property, he and his son live constantly in the same place and share the same occupations. Habit and necessity bring them together and force them into constant contact. The inevitable result is a kind of familiar intimacy, which makes authority less absolute and can hardly be reconciled with outward forms of respect. Now in democratic countries the class of those who hold small fortunes is precisely the class that gives strength to the ideas, and a particular direction to the mores, of the community. That class makes its opinions prevail as universally as its will, and even those most inclined to resist its commands are carried along in the end by its example. I have known eager opponents of democracy who let their children address them with perfect colloquial equality.

problem: 'most democratic state of society' softened to 'thoroughly democratic'
replacement: No free communities have ever existed without morals, and, as I observed in the earlier part of this work, morals are the work of woman. Whatever affects the condition of women, their habits and their opinions, therefore has great political importance in my eyes. Among almost all Protestant nations, young women are far more in charge of their own actions than they are in Catholic countries. This independence is greater still in Protestant countries like England, which have kept or gained the right of self-government; there, political habits and religious opinions bring the spirit of freedom into the domestic circle. In the United States, the doctrines of Protestantism are joined with great political freedom and a most democratic state of society, and nowhere are young women left so early or so completely to their own guidance. Long before an American girl reaches marriageable age, her release from her mother’s control begins. She has hardly stopped being a child when she already thinks for herself, speaks freely and acts on her own impulse. The great scene of the world lies constantly open before her. Far from being hidden from her, it is shown to her more fully every day, and she is taught to look at it with a steady and calm gaze. So the vices and dangers of society are revealed to her early. She sees them clearly, looks at them without illusions and faces them without fear, for she is full of reliance on her own strength, and everyone around her seems to share that reliance. An American girl almost never shows the virginal bloom amid youthful desires, or the innocent, artless grace that usually accompanies the European woman in the passage from girlhood to youth. It is rare for an American woman, at any age, to show childish timidity or ignorance. Like the young women of Europe, she wants to please, but she knows exactly what pleasing costs. If she does not give herself up to evil, at least she knows that it exists, and she is notable more for purity of conduct than for chastity of mind. I have often been surprised, and almost alarmed, by the remarkable skill and happy boldness with which young women in America manage their thoughts and their words through all the difficulties of a stimulating conversation. A philosopher would have stumbled at every step along the narrow path they walked without accident and without effort. It is easy to see that even in the independence of early youth, an American woman is always mistress of herself. She enjoys every permitted pleasure without surrendering to any of them, and her reason never lets the reins of self-guidance fall, though it often seems to hold them loosely.
